title: Participant Prime Playbook — personal lab notebook
content:
Context / intent:
This is a personal lab notebook exploring a lightweight client-side "prime" concept: small, targeted warmup requests sent ahead of an interactive LLM call to reduce SLO violations and cold-cache latency while keeping token cost predictable. The idea sits between full prefix caching and ad-hoc prefetch — an opt-in per-client "participant prime" layer that can be shaped by client heuristics and budget.

High-level goals:
- Reduce first-token / first-burst latency in multi-participant sessions (group chat, collaborative docs).
- Keep extra token overhead bounded (per-session microbudget).
- Make primes cheap and retry-safe; no heavy state commitments on server.
- Allow per-participant tailoring (role, recentness, sensitivity).

Key assumptions:
- Serving runtime exposes fast prefix (KV) priming API that accepts short sequences to populate KV cache without creating a long-lived expensive state.
- Client can predict "near future" inputs with low to moderate accuracy (e.g., message starters, common follow-ups).
- We can accept small potential for waste (some primes won't help) but must cap cost.

Design sketch: participant-prime primitive
- API: POST /v1/sessions/{sid}/primes (or a single batch endpoint for many participants)
- Semantics: best-effort, idempotent, nonblocking, cost-accounted. Server treats primes as warmup-only; they do not produce billing tokens for full generation results (only a small prebill or separate prime-credit).

Example request (draft shape):
{
  "session_id": "sid_4b2f",
  "participant_id": "user:alice",
  "role_hint": "writer",
  "primes": [
    {"id":"p-1","type":"prefix","tokens":"Summarize the last message in one line","priority":10},
    {"id":"p-2","type":"phrase","tokens":"Thanks! Can you also" ,"priority":5}
  ],
  "budget_tokens": 16,
  "budget_ms": 80,
  "ttl_ms": 300000  // how long server should keep priming context warm for this session (ms)
}

Notes on fields:
- budget_tokens: hard cap per participant per interval (enforced).
- budget_ms: suggestion for how long the runtime should bias scheduling the prime before next real request.
- ttl_ms: expiry for the warmed KV entries; server may evict earlier.
- priority: local hint used by server-side scheduler to order primes when capacity is constrained.

Server response (minimal):
{
  "status":"accepted",
  "accepted_primes": ["p-1","p-2"],
  "estimated_warm_ms": 28
}

Operational considerations:
- Attribution / billing: treat primes differently (tiny unit charge) or as part of a pre-allocated prime-credit for Dedicated customers. Need accounting for experiments.
- Security / privacy: clients might send sensitive context; require opt-in, encryption-in-transit and KMS tagging for private deployments. Add flag "sensitive": true to mark primes that should not be stored beyond volatile cache.
- Backpressure: if runtime is at capacity, server should return 429 with a backoff window and optionally a fallback token to request on next user message.

Heuristics catalog (client-side):
- Idle-reheat: when user is active in session but has been idle < Xs, send a short, high-priority prime containing last message summary.
- Typing-probe: when client detects typing start, send a phrase-prime with common continuations for the detected language/intent.
- Role-presets: assistant vs user vs reviewer — priming sequences chosen from small curated templates per role.
- Confidence-gated: only prime when the local model/heuristic predicts > P% chance next message will need inference.
- Cost-smoothing: spread primes across participants with a round-robin credit scheduler to avoid noisy spikes.

Data flow ASCII diagram:

client (browser/mobile)
  |--(prime request)--> ingress (api layer)
  |                    -> routing/policy (checks budget, team plan)
  |                    -> runtime scheduler (assigns micro-work to GPU host)
  |                    -> KV cache warmed on host(s)
  |--(real user request)--> runtime (benefits from warmed cache)

Edge cases / failure modes:
- Over-priming: many clients prime at once causing transient spike. Mitigation: admission control + randomized jitter + quota.
- Stale primes: primes for long-idle sessions might be worthless; enforce ttl and cheap invalidation.
- Cross-tenant leakage risk for shared hosts: primes must be tenant-scoped and encrypted.
- Inconsistent warm state across multi-host routing: consider tagging primes with "affinity_hint" to prefer same host for near-term requests.

Experiment matrix (initial A/B):
- Variant A: no primes (baseline).
- Variant B: aggressive primes (budget_tokens=32, ttl=5min) for active participants.
- Variant C: conservative primes (budget_tokens=8, ttl=2min) with confidence gating.
Metrics to track:
- p95 first-token latency on first interactive request after idle.
- Prime cost per active user (tokens + cycles).
- Fraction of primes that yielded >10% latency improvement.
- SLO violations avoided vs extra cost.

Open questions / TODOs:
- How to surface prime costs in existing token-level billing UI? Add per-session prime bucket?
- Rollout gating: only on Dedicated or specific models? Should be allowed on hosted API with per-customer opt-in.
- Should primes be allowed to execute lightweight scoring only (cheap model) vs full-generation prime?
- Formal API shape for batch multi-participant primes (send N primes in one call).

Notes to self:
- Prototype client heuristics in small JS lib (prefetch-heuristics.js) and run internal simulation (10k sessions) to measure wasted prime rate.
- Talk to infra about adding a small "prime" priority queue in runtime scheduler.
- Check with privacy for guidance on short-lived KV retention policies.

Quick sketch of a possible config schema (YAML style, rough):

prime_policy:
  enabled: true
  per_participant_budget_tokens: 12
  global_concurrency_limit: 200
  backpressure:
    jitter_ms: 500
    retry_after_s: 2
  affinity_hint_enabled: true

-- end --

(unfinished; this is a working scratchpad. keep iteration notes here.)
